content: 1. The use of oral ivermectin for scabies, compared to permethrin, showed a low-quality evidence base. The studies lacked proper confirmation of diagnosis, clear definitions of clinical cure, and consistent methodologies. Cure rates were often defined as greater than 50% improvement in lesion count, which is not a robust measure. 2. When comparing oral ivermectin with antihistamines to permethrin with antihistamines for scabies, the evidence quality was very low. The clinical cure rate was not clearly defined, and there were inconsistencies in the methodology, such as mentioning a single dose in one section and repeated doses in another. 3. Comparing oral ivermectin (two applications) to topical permethrin (two applications) for scabies also yielded very low-quality evidence. The studies were not blinded, and the definition of cure based on lesion count was unclear. Second doses were only given to non-responsive patients, introducing bias. 4. In studies comparing topical permethrin (two applications) to oral ivermectin (two applications) for scabies, the evidence was of very low quality. Cure was defined as the absence of new lesions, which is not a rigorous standard. The studies were not blinded, and the number of patients receiving azithromycin was not reported. 5. Comparing topical permethrin (two applications) to benzyl benzoate (two applications) for scabies also showed very low-quality evidence. The definition of cure was unclear, and the studies lacked blinding. Only patients who did not improve after one week received a second application. 6. The comparison of oral ivermectin (two applications) to benzyl benzoate (two applications) for scabies in HIV-positive patients was based on very low-quality evidence. The studies were observational and retrospective, with small sample sizes and unclear definitions of dermatological cure. 7. For HIV-positive patients with scabies, the use of oral ivermectin versus a combination of topical benzyl benzoate and oral ivermectin was supported by very low-quality evidence. The studies were retrospective, with small populations and unclear methodologies. 8. The use of ivermectin versus combined therapy (ivermectin, permethrin, salicylic acid) for crusted scabies was based on very low-quality evidence. Repeated doses were administered to unresponsive patients, and the combination group received three doses of ivermectin only when single doses failed. 9. Comparing ivermectin (single dose) to benzyl benzoate (two applications) for scabies showed low-quality evidence. The studies were not blinded, and no HIV testing or immunological assays were performed before or after treatment. 10. For the management of oropharyngeal candidiasis associated with HIV, fluconazole versus ketoconazole showed low-quality evidence. Randomization methods were not described, and there was baseline imbalance. The confidence intervals were wide and included null effects. 11. Comparing fluconazole to itraconazole for oral candidiasis in HIV-infected individuals showed very low-quality evidence. There was a lack of blinding, heterogeneity in the studies, and wide confidence intervals that included null effects. 12. The comparison of fluconazole to clotrimazole for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was based on low-quality evidence. The studies lacked blinding, and the total number of events was less than 300, reducing the reliability of the findings. 13. Comparing fluconazole to fluconazole stat for oropharyngeal candidiasis showed moderate-quality evidence. However, allocation concealment and random sequence generation were not reported, and the sample size was small. 14. The use of fluconazole versus nystatin for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was supported by low-quality evidence. Randomization and allocation concealment were not reported, and the studies were single-blinded. 15. Comparing itraconazole to clotrimazole for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed very low-quality evidence. The studies lacked proper allocation concealment and blinding, and the confidence intervals included null effects. 16. The use of melaleuca alcohol-free oral solution versus alcohol-based oral solution for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was based on very low-quality evidence. The sample size was small, and randomization and blinding were not reported. 17. Comparing amphotericin fat emulsion to glucose solution for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed very low-quality evidence. The studies lacked blinding, and the sample size was small with wide confidence intervals. 18. The comparison of ketoconazole to miconazole for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was based on low-quality evidence. Allocation concealment and blinding were unclear, and the effect size was small. 19. Comparing gentian violet to ketoconazole for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed very low-quality evidence. The studies were small, and the confidence intervals included null effects. 20. The use of gentian violet versus nystatin for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was supported by very low-quality evidence. The studies were small, with less than 300 events, and lacked blinding. 21. Comparing ketoconazole to nystatin for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed very low-quality evidence. The studies were small, with less than 300 events, and lacked blinding. 22. The use of caspofungin versus amphotericin B for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was based on very low-quality evidence. The studies had small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. 23. Comparing posaconazole to fluconazole for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed low-quality evidence. Randomization methods were unclear, and the studies had small sample sizes with wide confidence intervals. 24. The use of lemon juice versus gentian violet for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was supported by very low-quality evidence. The studies were small, with less than 300 events, and lacked blinding. 25. Comparing lemon grass to gentian violet for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients showed very low-quality evidence. The studies were small, with less than 300 events, and the confidence intervals included null effects. 26. The use of lemon juice versus lemon grass for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients was based on very low-quality evidence. The studies lacked blinding and had small sample sizes with wide confidence intervals. 27.
